extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, patent drafters, and inventors preparing patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting a patent specification to avoid narrowing claim construction and creating unintended disclaimers; focuses on phrasing, disclosures, definitions, and background content. Advice is aimed at producing specifications that support broader claim scope and survive litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification determines claim meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms get their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification; the spec is the dictionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit decisions over the last decade have repeatedly turned on what the specification did or did not say (e.g., Phillips v. AWH (2005, en banc)). Treat the specification as the primary source for construing claim terms because courts will look to it when determining ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid singular framing of 'the invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the spec says 'the present invention is X' or 'the invention requires Y,' courts may construe every claim as limited to X or Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present features as universally required by 'the invention' because statements framed that way can be used to narrowly construe all claims. Example: SciMed v. Advanced Cardiovascular (Fed. Cir. 2001) where language describing a coaxial design led to excluding other designs such as dual-lumen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'embodiments' rather than defining 'the invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to 'an embodiment,' 'one example,' 'in some implementations,' or 'a non-limiting example' so the disclosure reads as optional examples instead of a single definition of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame disclosures as illustrative embodiments to avoid implying that any single disclosed example is the only way to practice the invention. This helps prevent limiting claim construction to the disclosed example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmatively define terms when useful (be your own lexicographer)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a claim term to have a specific meaning, define it explicitly in the specification (e.g., 'As used herein, the term "X" means ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts respect express definitions provided in the spec. Use clear, affirmative definitions to control claim term meaning when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid definition by negative implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write 'in contrast to prior systems, which used Y, the present system uses X' because that can be read as disclaiming Y from the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe what your system does without negatively contrasting it with prior art. Negative comparisons can be interpreted as an express exclusion of alternatives and narrow the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose ranges rather than single numeric values
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prototype runs at 50 Hz, the spec should say 'between approximately 30 Hz and 100 Hz, e.g., 50 Hz.' Single values invite narrow construction; disclosed ranges support broader claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ranges and examples rather than only a single data point to avoid implying that the invention is limited to that exact value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose multiple embodiments across different use cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that describes only one product is implicitly limited to that product; describing the invention in multiple fields and with multiple embodiments supports broader construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include varied examples and embodiments (e.g., applying the invention to three different fields with three different embodiments) to demonstrate breadth and avoid limiting the claims to a single implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the background concise and factual; avoid disparaging prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Long background sections that disparage prior art create estoppel and admissions under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Avoid characterizing prior art as having 'drawbacks' or 'deficiencies' you have solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the background short and factual. Overly negative descriptions of prior art can be quoted against you in litigation and used to limit claim scope or support obviousness findings.
